Recent work cautions against equating ranking accuracy with useful order modeling. [Oh and Cho (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) propose measuring excessive recency emphasis and report improvements from mitigating it. [Liu et al. (RecSys 2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748042) show that unrestricted history shuffling mixes user-order effects with item-availability effects; constrained shuffling respects items’ first appearances. [Petrov et al. (2026)](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling) find history-aware pairwise transition models outperform SASRec and eSASRec reproductions on four of five benchmarks. Their results distinguish benefits from earlier history, recency weighting, and joint contextualization; strong scores alone do not establish higher-order sequence use.

A practical diagnostic design suggested by these findings: freeze the trained model and candidate set; remove recent interactions, repeated occurrences, or explicitly defined isolated events; compare each intervention with equal-size random removals, additionally matching position or popularity where feasible. Shuffle only valid history positions, with a separate last-item-preserving shuffle to distinguish terminal-item reliance from broader order sensitivity. Measure paired changes in target rank, HR@10, top-10 overlap, and recommendation popularity, reporting uncertainty and category-specific effects. Popularity-only, last-item, and recency-weighted pairwise controls help separate sequence dependence from simpler signals. Connect observed sensitivity to positional embeddings, attention, and next-item supervision through controlled component ablations or retraining; prediction perturbations alone cannot identify which component learned the behavior. Removal effects assess model dependence and explanation faithfulness, but padding changes, position shifts, and implausible histories can confound them. These are computational interventions, not evidence of real-world causal effects on user preferences.
